Opinion: Amendment 3 is appealing, but likely comes at a high cost

By CNW Contributor·Friday, October 16, 2026·3 min read
Key Points(5)
  • While most Floridians are focused on the highly competitive races for governor and the U.S.
  • 3 general election, there is another ballot item of critical importance that voters should pay close attention to and try not to overlook: Florida Amendment 3.
  • The amendment has distinct implications for the cost of living for Florida homeowners and the revenue budgets of just about every county and city in the state.
  • Amendment 3 is a proposed constitutional change to Florida’s property tax system.
  • If passed, meaning it receives approval from at least 60% of Florida voters, it would increase the state’s homestead exemption.

While most Floridians are focused on the highly competitive races for governor and the U.S. Senate in the Nov. 3 general election, there is another ballot item of critical importance that voters should pay close attention to and try not to overlook: Florida Amendment 3.

The amendment has distinct implications for the cost of living for Florida homeowners and the revenue budgets of just about every county and city in the state.

Advertisement

Amendment 3 is a proposed constitutional change to Florida’s property tax system. If passed, meaning it receives approval from at least 60% of Florida voters, it would increase the state’s homestead exemption. The exemption for property taxes on a qualifying primary residence would rise to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments afterward.

Advertisement

Advertisement

The annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties, including rental and commercial properties, would fall from 10% to 5%.

The amendment would restrict how property tax revenue is used while allowing some additional exemptions and leaving important spending decisions to local governments and state lawmakers.

The school property tax exemption would not increase in the same way, so homeowners would continue to pay school property taxes.

Advertisement

Advertisement

Supporters of the amendment claim Florida homeowners need relief from rising property taxes. A larger exemption could reduce the tax burden on eligible owner-occupied homes, while the lower assessment cap could help businesses and other property owners manage future increases.

Advertisement

Advertisement

On the other hand, opponents argue that local governments depend on property taxes to fund police, fire rescue, emergency services, roads, parks and other services. Lower revenues could lead to service reductions, higher fees or pressure to raise other taxes. The amendment does not guarantee a minimum level of funding for police or fire departments.

An important distinction is that a reduction in property taxes does not necessarily mean an equal reduction in a homeowner’s total cost of living. The ultimate impact depends on the tax savings, changes in local services and whether other fees or taxes rise.

Advertisement

According to a poll commissioned by Associated Industries of Florida, a business organization with an interest in the issue, as of Oct. 14, there was strong support for the amendment, with 53% saying they would vote yes and 28% saying they would vote no. The remaining 19% were undecided.

The critical point is that Florida requires 60% approval for a constitutional amendment to pass, not a simple majority. The reported 53% support is therefore seven percentage points short of the required threshold.

Over the next three weeks, undecided voters are certain to be relentlessly targeted by campaigns seeking to persuade them to support or oppose the amendment. Are these voters undecided because they cannot make up their minds about whether to take advantage of the property tax savings and keep more money in their pockets, or whether to be concerned about losing local services?

Opponents, in their campaigns, are suggesting that the savings are overstated because they depend on the assessed values of homeowners’ properties and local tax rates, and because school property taxes would remain. They are also questioning who would bear the cost of the revenue reduction. Local governments might have to reduce services, increase fees or adjust taxes elsewhere. The amendment does not guarantee that public safety budgets will be preserved.

For homeowners, immediate tax savings could be meaningful, but the longer-term effects on municipal finances and other taxpayers also deserve attention.

Once a constitutional amendment is passed, reversing it is not easy. Doing so would require another constitutional amendment approved by at least 60% of voters.

In the current difficult economic climate, property tax savings can be very appealing to voters. But should those savings come at the expense of vital services provided by local governments?

Because some of these services are essential to most Floridians, and the amendment’s proponents have not provided a meaningful explanation of how municipal services would be funded, this newspaper finds it difficult to support the measure.

Broward schools administrator fired over laptop procurement investigation

By Joanne Clark·Thursday, October 15, 2026
Key Points(5)
  • A Broward schools administrator accused by the county’s top watchdog of mismanaging the purchase of laptops and misleading the School Board has been fired.
  • The firing of Jennifer Andreu came despite pleas for leniency from many of her supporters, who told School Board members on Tuesday she had done nothing to warrant the action.
  • Andreu denies wrongdoing.
  • Andreu was the school district’s executive director of operations from 2023 to early 2026, a period when Broward’s Office of Inspector General scrutinized three efforts to select vendors for laptop purchases and deployment.
  • She was moved to a job overseeing economic development and compliance earlier this year.

Jamaican American school administrator Jennifer Andreu has been fired by the Broward County School Board following an investigation into the district’s laptop procurement process that found she and other employees mismanaged the process and misled board members.

The board voted 6-3 on Tuesday to terminate Andreu, who served as the school district’s executive director of operations from 2023 to early 2026. Board members Adam Cervera, Jeff Holness and Nora Rupert voted against the termination.

The decision came despite pleas for leniency from supporters who addressed the board, arguing that Andreu had done nothing to warrant her dismissal. Andreu has denied wrongdoing.

The Broward Office of Inspector General released its investigation on Sept. 30 after examining three efforts to select vendors for laptop purchases and deployment. The report concluded that, while Andreu and some other employees “did not engage in misconduct or gross mismanagement, they mismanaged the procurement process and, in the course of doing so, misled the School Board.”

Andreu was moved from her operations role to a position overseeing economic development and compliance earlier this year.

Superintendent defends disciplinary action

During his superintendent’s report on Tuesday, before the board discussed Andreu’s employment, Superintendent Howard Hepburn said the inspector general’s findings highlighted significant problems that the district needed to address.

“The concerns identified in this report are unacceptable, and we are taking action. Public trust is earned through our actions, not simply our words,” Hepburn told the board.

“Any employee found to have knowingly misled the School Board, violated district policies, or broken the law will face swift and appropriate disciplinary action up to and including termination,” he added.

During the discussion, board member Jeff Holness questioned the decision-making process.

“Rush decision or a harsh decision?” Holness asked.

“This is not a rush or a harsh decision,” Hepburn responded.

Broward Teachers Union President Anna Fusco also challenged the process used to terminate Andreu, arguing that the district had not followed proper procedures.

“This due process was not done accurately, it was not done right,” Fusco said while addressing the board.

Andreu considers appeal

Speaking to the South Florida Sun Sentinel after the meeting, Andreu said she was disappointed by the board’s decision and was considering her options to challenge the termination.

“I’m deeply disappointed by the board’s decision,” Andreu said. “I did nothing to warrant termination and stand by my nearly 30 years of public service and integrity.”

She told the newspaper that she was reviewing options to “continue defending my reputation,” including appealing the decision to Florida’s Division of Administrative Hearings.

The termination follows months of scrutiny over the district’s laptop procurement efforts and raises questions about accountability in the management of public education resources.

Andreu maintains that she did not engage in conduct warranting dismissal, while district leadership has said disciplinary action is necessary to address the concerns identified by the inspector general.
